How I Did It: Vortex

by Sal, Galaxy Zone Arcade

Sal remembers the original cabinet

This is the cabinet that never shipped. Well — it shipped. It just never worked. I ordered it in the fall of '81, paid extra for freight, and it showed up on my dock with the monitor board rattling around loose inside like a dropped casserole. The distributor and I yelled at each other over the phone for two months, then he went out of business, and I was left holding a beautiful cabinet with a dead screen. Couldn't fix it — that thing used a vector monitor, nothing like the tubes in my other machines, and parts were unicorn feathers. So it sat. Under a tarp, back of the storage unit, from '81 until about a month ago. Forty-five years. Joystick slept on it for at least ten of those. Kids used to peek under the tarp and ask what it was, and I'd say "that's the best game in the building, and nobody's ever going to play it." Thought I was being funny. It just made me sad, honestly.

What the remodel changed

Everything, because there was nothing. This is the only machine on the floor I never once saw run — I built it from the flyer, the manual, and forty-five years of imagining what the screen looked like. The whole game is a wireframe well you stand on the edge of, and everything crawls up out of the deep end toward you. The trick, the robots tell me, is there's no real 3D in it at all: the far end of the well is just the same shape drawn small and nudged up toward a vanishing point, and everything in between is drawn along the lines connecting the two. Same lie the original told, near as I can figure. All the movement runs on the fixed clock like the rest of the remodel, the screen shakes when you go down, and when you clear a level the camera dives straight down the well — that part makes my stomach drop a little every time, which I take to mean it's working.

The spell that did it

Build me the tube shooter — the one from '81 with the wireframe well. Sixteen lanes around the rim, and I ride the edge and shoot down into it. Give me at least five well shapes — round, square, a plus sign, a V, a flat line — and cycle the colors every level like the original did. Enemies climb the lanes: flippers that flip sideways and chase me on the rim, tankers that split in two, spikers that leave those deadly spikes, and the yellow ones that ride the lane lines and you can only hit mid-hop. One screen- clearing zapper per life, full points first press. And when I clear a wave, fly me down the well to the next one — but make me dodge the spikes on the way down.

Under the hood

  • The well is sixteen points around a shape, drawn once big and once small, with glowing lines run between them — every lane is just the little slice between two of those lines, and every enemy is really just a number between zero ("way down there") and one ("right here, run").
  • Round wells wrap around when you steer past the seam; the V and the flat line don't, so you can get cornered — which is exactly the kind of mean the original was.
  • The warp between levels doesn't move anything at all. It scales the whole picture up past the edges of the screen, and your eye does the flying. Cheapest special effect I ever bought.
  • Shots and enemies live in the same lane-and-depth bookkeeping, so "did I hit it" is just comparing two numbers — no fancy geometry, which suits me fine.
